The core insight is that the Industrial Revolution's foundational technologies imposed hard physical constraints on spatial organization. Steam engines exhibited strong economies of scale, necessitating centralization, while textile machinery was modular and lightweight. The mechanical transmission systems—shafts, belts, and pulleys—served as the glue binding dispersed machines into a unified production network. These components introduced discrete failure modes: misalignment causing wear, slack leading to energy loss, and overloading resulting in catastrophic breakage. Mathematically, this forms a directed acyclic graph where the prime mover is the root node, distributing power through a hierarchical tree structure to leaf nodes representing individual looms or spindles. The transition to distributed electric motors decouples this rigidity, enabling modular reconfiguration. This abstraction maps cleanly to modern algorithmic trading networks, where a central execution venue (prime mover) feeds liquidity to dispersed order books (machines), with communication latency (transmission) dictating optimal colocation strategies.
